questions.question: A PM orders three bets by which one is most ready to start. What is the strategic cost of this ordering rule?
options: Readiness ordering usually delays the highest-value work
It makes the delivery schedule harder to communicate to stakeholders
It ignores effort estimates, so capacity gets overcommitted
It decides what you will know at each commitment, and which commitments remain available, without anyone treating that as a decision
questions.explanation: Order determines the information available at each commitment and which later moves are still open, both of which are strategic. A is the tempting answer because it sounds like prioritization discipline, but the deeper cost is not value ordering — it is committing while still ignorant and closing doors you have not yet decided you can lose.

questions.question: Which uncertainty most deserves to be retired first?
options: How much slower large workspaces feel to users, where either answer leads to the same fix
Whether the audience you committed to actually has the problem, where a negative answer invalidates the position
Which of two implementations of a feature performs better under load
How competitors will price a similar capability next year
questions.explanation: Decision relevance means different resolutions lead to different next moves, and a false audience claim would stop the whole position. A is the tempting distractor: the uncertainty is genuinely large and feels important, but if both answers lead to the same fix, resolving it changes nothing.

questions.question: Noted's dependency loses support in 10 weeks and the migration is estimated at three to five weeks with wide uncertainty. How is the latest start date derived?
options: Ten weeks minus the midpoint estimate, since that is the expected duration
Ten weeks minus the optimistic estimate, leaving room to fund other bets first
Ten weeks minus the pessimistic estimate minus time to react if the estimate is wrong
It cannot be derived, because nothing breaks at the end-of-support date
questions.explanation: The pessimistic estimate plus reaction time is what makes the date survivable when the estimate proves wrong, and the estimate is explicitly wide. D is tempting because the case says nothing breaks immediately, but an exposure that accumulates rather than detonates still has a start date you can miss.

questions.question: A team says it will keep two architectural options open through the quarter. What must be stated for this to count as optionality rather than avoidance?
options: The carrying cost of holding the option, and the condition under which it would be exercised
The probability that each option is chosen, so the work can be weighted
A commitment to decide by the end of the quarter
Which engineer owns each option
questions.explanation: An option with no named exercise condition is an unresolved decision, and one with an unstated carrying cost looks free when it is not. C is the tempting answer, because a decision date feels like rigor, but a date without an exercise condition just relocates the same avoidance to a later meeting.

questions.question: A PM plans to run a learning step whose result will not be measurable until three weeks after the following commitment begins. What does the boundary of this model say?
options: Proceed, since partial signals will still inform the second commitment
The ordering provides no information benefit, so either move the step earlier or stop calling it a learning sequence
Shorten the measurement window so the result arrives in time
Run both steps in parallel to save calendar time
questions.explanation: Sequencing pays off only when a result is observable before the next commitment; otherwise the work has been split, not sequenced. C is the tempting fix, and it is often worse: shortening the window to fit the plan produces a number on time that cannot support the claim it was meant to test.
